Trying to Conceive

Progesterone: why levels change and what a test can tell you

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Progesterone is a hormone involved in the menstrual cycle and pregnancy. Its level naturally changes rather than staying at one ideal number. Before interpreting a result as high or low, a clinician needs to know when the sample was taken, whether ovulation or pregnancy is likely, and whether you are using hormone treatment.

Follow the normal cycle rather than a fixed day

After ovulation, the follicle that released the egg becomes the corpus luteum and produces progesterone. The hormone helps prepare the uterine lining for implantation. If pregnancy does not occur, hormone levels fall and the lining is shed as a period.

Ovulation does not happen on day 14 in every cycle. A progesterone test intended to assess recent ovulation needs timing appropriate to your cycle, rather than an automatic calendar date. Irregular cycles make interpretation more complicated.

In early pregnancy, signals from the developing pregnancy help maintain the corpus luteum. The placenta later takes over much of progesterone production. This is a gradual transition, not a reason to change prescribed treatment at a self-selected week.

Luteinising hormone, or LH, is released by the pituitary and helps trigger ovulation and formation of the corpus luteum. After implantation, hCG from pregnancy-related tissue supports the corpus luteum until placental hormone production becomes established, broadly during the first trimester. Progesterone changes the estrogen-primed lining so it can support implantation; it does not fertilise the egg.

Progesterone also contributes to uterine quietness, immune adaptation and breast development. Together with other hormones it suppresses further ovulation during pregnancy. High pregnancy progesterone helps prepare the breasts, while its fall after placental delivery is part of the transition to abundant milk production; more progesterone is not a way to increase milk supply.

One low result does not explain every fertility problem

Progesterone is released in pulses, so a blood level can change substantially over a short time. A suitably interpreted measurement may support that ovulation occurred, but one value cannot reliably grade egg quality, overall fertility or the quality of an entire luteal phase.

The term luteal phase deficiency describes a proposed problem with progesterone exposure or response after ovulation. Its diagnosis and significance remain debated. Current specialist guidance does not identify one reliable test that separates fertile from infertile people on this basis.

If you are having difficulty conceiving or repeated losses, assessment should consider the wider history and both partners where relevant. It should not begin and end with a single hormone result.

Symptoms are not a progesterone deficiency checklist

Irregular bleeding, acne, dry skin, fatigue and mood changes have many possible explanations. They do not establish a deficiency, and cracked heels or brittle nails are not a substitute for an appropriate medical assessment.

Conditions that disrupt ovulation can also change progesterone patterns. This does not mean low progesterone itself causes every case of polycystic ovary syndrome, insulin resistance or weight gain. A test result may reflect a wider process rather than being its root cause.

Likewise, a high level may be expected after ovulation, during pregnancy or with treatment. An unexpected result needs interpretation; it is neither always harmless nor a diagnosis of an ovarian tumor by itself.

Persistent high results outside the expected cycle or treatment context can sometimes prompt assessment of ovarian cysts or uncommon ovarian or adrenal conditions, including congenital adrenal hyperplasia. They are possible reasons to investigate, not symptoms that diagnose a tumour. Research on hormone effects and ovarian-cancer risk does not justify taking progesterone to prevent cancer without a clinical indication.

Ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, preterm birth and hypertensive disorders cannot be diagnosed as “progesterone deficiency” from a symptom list. Low levels may accompany some failing pregnancies rather than explain why they failed. Likewise, sugar cravings, weight gain or depression need a broader assessment than simply trying to raise this hormone.

Prescribed progesterone has specific uses

Progesterone support is used in some fertility-treatment protocols. Selected early-pregnancy situations may also benefit. For example, NICE recommends a particular vaginal preparation for people with early bleeding, a previous miscarriage and an intrauterine pregnancy confirmed on ultrasound. That is a defined clinical indication, not a recommendation for everyone trying to conceive.

Do not start, stop or change a prescribed course from an online result or symptom list. Ask why it was prescribed, how to use it, what side effects to report and when it should be reviewed. Treatment after assisted reproduction is a different setting from supplementing an otherwise natural cycle.

Bleeding or pain in pregnancy still needs assessment. A progesterone result cannot locate the pregnancy or safely rule out an ectopic pregnancy; it must not delay appropriate scans and clinical review.

Food supports health without replacing hormone treatment

A varied diet can meet nutritional needs, but the listed foods, vitamins and minerals cannot be relied on to raise progesterone to a chosen level. There is no proven food combination that corrects every cycle or prevents miscarriage.

Avoid high-dose supplements or unregulated hormone creams sold as a natural way to balance hormones. Bring product details to your clinician. If testing is recommended, confirm its purpose and timing, then discuss the result in context rather than comparing it with a single internet target.

Foods often advertised for hormone balance include nuts, poultry, citrus, leafy greens, peppers, cabbage, beans, broccoli, wheat germ, pumpkin, dark chocolate, salmon, shrimp and oats. Many can contribute useful nutrients within pregnancy food-safety guidance, but they are not progesterone replacement. Vitamin C, zinc, vitamin E and L-arginine supplements also lack a universal role in correcting a low progesterone test; unnecessary high doses can carry risks.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

ASRM emphasises pulsatile progesterone secretion and the limits of one measurement for diagnosing luteal-phase problems.

Prescribed progesterone has specific fertility and selected pregnancy indications; timing, symptoms and scans guide its use.

How BeMama can help

Ask why a test or treatment is proposed, when the sample is informative and what result would change your care.

When to seek help

Pregnancy pain or bleeding needs assessment for its cause; do not use a hormone result or unregulated product to delay care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Progesterone changes through the cycle and pregnancy.
  • A single result cannot explain every fertility or miscarriage concern.
  • Treatment should have a specific indication; foods and supplements are not reliable hormone replacement.

Frequently asked questions

Should everyone test progesterone on day 21?

No. Timing depends on the cycle and the reason for testing. Ask your clinician when the sample will be informative.

Can a low progesterone result diagnose an ectopic pregnancy?

No. It cannot establish pregnancy location. Pain or bleeding may require ultrasound, other tests and clinical assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
